snippets.title: Pedal that sinks at a stop from master cylinder bypass
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. The brake pedal may slowly sink toward the floor while held at a stop, with no external leak, because fluid bypasses the master cylinder seals. With the engine off, pump the brake pedal several times to use up booster reserve. Apply steady, moderate pressure to the pedal and hold it for one minute. Repair: replace the master cylinder and bleed the system.

snippets.title: Cool vent air from a skipping blend door actuator
snippets.text: Applies to all models. Vent temperature may stay cool, with a clicking noise behind the dash, because the blend door actuator skips or stops short of full hot. With the engine warm, run the climate control from full cold to full hot while listening behind the center of the dash. The actuator should move smoothly through its full travel without clicking or stopping short. Repair: replace the blend door actuator and recalibrate it.

snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. A steering wheel shake that occurs only when braking from highway speed, and is absent when cruising, usually comes from front rotor thickness variation. Measure rotor runout and thickness variation. Repair: replace or refinish the front rotors.

snippets.title: Weak heat in cold weather from a thermostat stuck open
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.4L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. From a cold start, idle the engine and watch coolant temperature on a scan tool while feeling the upper radiator hose. The hose should stay cool until about 195 deg F and warm quickly after that. Repair: replace the thermostat and gasket.

A pump that does not run leaves the heater core without flow at idle.

snippets.title: Steering wheel shake at highway speed from wheel imbalance
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. A steering wheel shake that peaks in a narrow band such as 60-70 mph may come from wheel and tire assemblies that are out of balance or have high road-force variation. Check each wheel and tire assembly on a road-force balancer. Static and dynamic imbalance should be under 0.25 oz, and road-force variation should be under about 20 lb for passenger tires. Repair: rebalance the assemblies and match-mount any tire with high road force.

snippets.title: Starter circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. With a helper holding the ignition in the start position, measure voltage drop from the battery positive post to the starter B+ terminal, and from the battery negative post to the engine block. Each side should be under 0.5 V. A higher drop means the starter cannot draw enough current to turn the engine, even when the battery is charged.

snippets.title: Battery voltage during a start attempt
snippets.text: Connect a meter across the battery posts and watch the reading while a helper attempts to start the engine. Voltage should not fall below 9.6 V. A battery that collapses below that value cannot power the starter even if dash lights look bright with the key on.

snippets.text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. The starter may intermittently fail to engage because of a weak starter relay in the underhood fuse block. Swap the starter relay with an identical relay and retest. Repair: replace the starter relay.

Pins should move freely by hand through their full travel. Repair: clean and lubricate the pins, or fit new pins and boots.

snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip. Fluid with more than 3 percent water has a reduced boiling point and can vaporize in the calipers, producing a soft pedal. Fluid that is dark or cloudy also indicates contamination.

messages.content: My midsize sedan is a 2016 with the 3.5L V6 and 74k on the clock. The pedal feels mushy all the time, even on flat roads around town. The brake light on the dash is off, and nothing has been done to the brakes in over a year. What's the first thing to look at?
Start with this: check the reservoir level and inspect each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness [SEC 11.17].
Can't you just tell me what to replace? I'd rather not run tests.
Naming a part now would be a guess. Check the reservoir level and inspect each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness [SEC 11.17].
OK, I tried it. Reservoir is at MAX and there are no wet spots at any wheel or at the master cylinder.
That rules that area out. With the engine off and the booster reserve pumped out, hold steady moderate pressure on the pedal for one minute and watch whether it slowly sinks [SEC 6.4].
Pedal stayed put under steady pressure for the whole minute. OK, so is it the brake line or not? I need a straight answer.
